articles.title_orig: China’s Big Three Airlines Face Annual Losses as Fuel Costs Rise
articles.title_zh: China’s Big Three Airlines Face Annual Losses as Fuel Costs Rise
articles.content_orig:
A global review of commercial flight
BEIJING — Air China (CA), China Eastern Airlines (MU) and China Southern Airlines (CZ) face full-year losses in 2026 after higher fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions weighed on their third-quarter results, Reuters reported on November 2 .
Analyst estimates compiled by London Stock Exchange Group point to a seventh consecutive annual net loss for Air China and China Eastern. China Southern is also forecast to lose money after returning to annual profit in 2025 for the first time since 2019.
According to Reuters, Air China’s third-quarter net profit fell 92.6% from a year earlier to 270.6m yuan. China Eastern earned 64m yuan, down 98.2% from the same quarter in 2025.
China Southern posted a quarterly net loss of 609m yuan, compared with a 3.84bn yuan profit a year earlier. All three carriers lost money over the first nine months of 2026, having been profitable in the corresponding period of 2025, Reuters reported.
The third quarter includes the peak summer travel season and is usually the strongest period for Chinese airlines. This year, even the small quarterly profits at Air China and China Eastern were insufficient to offset earlier losses.
The carriers entered 2026 after a prolonged recovery. Airways previously covered their first-half 2025 loss warnings , before China Southern’s return to annual profit.
Reuters reported that Chinese airlines hedge less of their fuel purchases than many Asian and European carriers, leaving them more exposed to price increases. Fuel hedging can limit the effect of price increases on an airline’s fuel bill.
Competition, including from high-speed rail, also weighed on domestic fares. In its April 8 research on the carriers , DBS said price-sensitive consumers constrained their ability to pass on higher fuel costs.
Using 2025 figures, DBS estimated that a 5% change in average jet fuel prices would change Air China’s fuel costs by about 2.5bn yuan and China Southern’s by 2.6bn yuan. Those sensitivities illustrate the scale of fuel exposure; they are not actual 2026 expenses.
Nathan Gee, head of Asia-Pacific transport research at BofA Global Research, told Reuters he expected Chinese airlines to remain loss-making in the seasonally weaker fourth quarter.
Gee said third-quarter earnings were slightly better than very low expectations. His checks suggested domestic fares were rising at double-digit rates year over year after the October Golden Week holiday as airlines restrained capacity. However, fuel remained a major pressure on earnings. He also said carriers were trying to increase flying hours per aircraft to control costs, but substantial cost reductions would be difficult.

articles.title_orig: Stocks rise as oil prices slide before midterms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks rise as oil prices slide before midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 7.7% to $104.66 a barrel as of 12:11 p.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate declined 7.3% to $96.50 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections.
The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.content_orig:
United States oil companies have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war on Iran, even as consumers pay much higher prices for key commodities, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may renew fighting after midterm elections .
The estimate, released by The New York Times, is a conservative evaluation based on the performance of 51 large US oil and gas companies in the six months from April through September. By contrast, in the same period in 2025 – when the prices of oil were lower prior to the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran – they collectively earned less than $47bn.
But the gains come as burgeoning living costs are crushing consumers. Americans have spent an extra $150bn on petrol and diesel since the war on Iran began on February 28, according to an analysis by Brown University ’s Climate Solutions Lab, which amounts to more than $1,150 per household.
The disparity has fuelled a political debate over who gains and who pays the price for the war. Responding to Trump, Democratic Representative Jim McGovern wrote on X: “We’re not making a ‘freaking fortune,’ we’re PAYING a ‘freaking fortune’.”
Naser al-Tamimi, a fellow at the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI) in Milan, Italy, said US energy companies have benefitted from the war in different ways. “Crude producers gain from higher oil prices, while refiners capture exceptional margins as diesel and other fuel supplies tighten,” he said.
Additionally, “damage to Middle Eastern and Russian refineries, disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipments , and sanctions-related trade frictions have intensified shortages”, while “relatively secure US facilities and access to discounted crude strengthen these gains”.
ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits of between $10bn and $15bn. While the gains are considerable, The New York Times found they generally remained below 2022 levels, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused oil prices to soar to roughly $100 a barrel and raised natural gas prices, compared with the current average of $90 from April through September.
American refining companies also reaped greater profits as global fuel supplies tightened and inventories depleted due to heavy damage to infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia. Valero Energy’s third-quarter profit increased more than sixfold, reaching $6.83bn. Phillips 66 announced its highest quarterly profit on record, with net income jumping to $5.62bn from $133m a year earlier.
Geoffrey Miller, geopolitical analyst and editor of the Gulf States Insights newsletter, said the US-Israel war with Iran “created the largest supply-side shock to global oil and refined products markets in years”.
Miller added that the war “created a risk premium that US-based operators are structurally well placed to monetise”. By contrast, Gulf producers were “hit hard by both higher costs and risks, along with physical damage, which makes their ability to benefit from the higher prices much more difficult”.
Tehran retaliated against the US-Israeli attack by launching missiles and drones at the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, found Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six GCC member states. Despite claims by Iranian officials that they were targeting US military facilities, they also hit energy infrastructure.
Iran also effectively blocked passage of most vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. In retaliation, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian oil and gas – the tit-for-tat steps raising the risks of transporting energy out of the crucial passageway.
Analysts warned of continued volatility until a durable political settlement between the US and Iran is reached. Oil prices dropped briefly in the summer after a memorandum of understanding was signed in June, but prices quickly soared again when talks broke down.
A more recent escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has further compounded the crisis: the Bab al-Mandeb strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which Saudi Arabia uses to export oil, is now also a theatre of war.
“In the short term, windfall profits will only strengthen oil company balance sheets and shareholder returns,” Miller said. “However, the big profits come with a major caveat. That’s because over the longer term, high oil prices risk harming economic growth prospects and could even contribute towards the outbreak of a recession, which would in turn be likely to lead to reduced demand for oil” and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank’s global economics and markets team in London, said it was likely that the prices of key energy products would remain high given the uncertainty about the duration of the war in Iran.
“Prices in all markets that have an exposure to this global supply shock – which includes the US – will face high prices also next year, and consumers will continue to feel this price pressure unless governments step in,” Schmit told Al Jazeera.
The US-led war on Iran has raised costs for oil, transport fuels, gas, electricity and food. According to the World Bank Group’s latest Commodity Markets Outlook, commodity prices are set to rise 23 percent this year, as disrupted grain shipments and the El Nino weather phenomenon also threaten harvests and food affordability.
The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization said on October 2 that world food commodity prices rose a further 1.5 percent in September, after reaching their highest level since late 2022 in August, amid adverse weather and trade disruptions in the Black Sea and Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has sought to blame high global fuel prices on Ukraine and pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries, even as Moscow continued to wage attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The US president has argued that a deal with Russia reversing years of sanctions would help lower diesel prices.
In the Gulf, analysts said higher oil prices will benefit exporters that can maintain shipments, but prolonged insecurity will continue to threaten supply reliability and investment.
“Gulf producers face years of reconstruction and pressure to diversify export routes,” ISPI’s al-Tamimi said. “A diplomatic settlement could ease prices, whereas renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran risk triggering another regional war, further disrupting Hormuz and prolonging shortages.”

articles.title_orig: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.title_zh: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.
Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum

articles.title_orig: Sectors bracing for a pivot as US midterm elections loom
articles.title_zh: Sectors bracing for a pivot as US midterm elections loom
articles.content_orig:
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: China releases timeline for lunar landing on the Moon, targeting "before 2030"
articles.title_zh: China releases timeline for lunar landing on the Moon, targeting "before 2030"
articles.content_orig:
Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”
China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.
According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.
Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.
NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.
But there are major questions surrounding the development of a lunar lander, for which both SpaceX and Blue Origin have multibillion-dollar development contracts. Depending on how these projects go, a US lunar landing could be delayed to 2030 or even later.
Although it is virtually impossible for outsiders to glean information about technical milestones achieved inside China’s space program, the country is clearly making credible progress toward reaching the Moon. For example, in August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency successfully tested a high-fidelity mock-up of its 26-ton Lanyue lunar lander. The test used giant tethers to simulate lunar gravity as the vehicle fired its main engines and fine-control thrusters to land on a cratered surface and take off from a location near Beijing.
Recently, the Mengzhou spacecraft for the 2027 test atop a Long March 10A rocket arrived at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan, China, where the mission will launch.
US government assessments of the Chinese space program are restricted, but lawmakers are clearly taking the threat seriously. In the last 12 months, the US Congress and White House have given broad latitude to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman to streamline the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon. He has moved swiftly to cancel the Lunar Gateway space station and planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket. And just last week, Isaacman announced plans to help Blue Origin develop a lunar lander by finding a way to boost the Orion spacecraft into low-lunar orbit.
“We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do,” he said at the time.
For a couple of years, it has been clear that China has made a major commitment to landing astronauts on the Moon, preferably before the United States returns to the lunar surface, to score a major geopolitical win. Beyond this near-term competition, both NASA and China’s space program are building capabilities to establish a long-term presence at the Moon’s South Pole. As part of this second phase of the contest, Isaacman committed NASA to the development of a base on the surface of the Moon over the next decade.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to criminalize Nvidia AI chip smuggling to China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to criminalize Nvidia AI chip smuggling to China
articles.content_orig:
Keep independent journalism alive
Taiwan is moving to criminalize the unauthorized export of advanced AI chips to China, aiming to close a loophole exposed when Nvidia-powered servers bought on the island reached Chinese buyers via Indonesia, Japan, and Hong Kong.
The Legislative Yuan’s Economics Committee held a public hearing on Monday on an amendment to the Foreign Trade Act proposed by lawmakers of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). It would ban exports of specified integrated circuits, key wafer materials, components and chipmaking equipment to mainland China without government approval.
Violators would face up to 10 years in prison and fines of NT$5 million to NT$10 million (US$155,000 to US$310,000), according to the proposed amendment. The same penalties would apply to anyone shipping controlled goods to China through a third country, while illegal gains would be confiscated.
The bill follows a case in which prosecutors in Keelung indicted nine people in August this year, including the general manager of Taiwanese firm Flying Tiger Technology and staff at the local units of Nvidia and Super Micro Computer. They allegedly diverted 74 Nvidia B300 servers to Chinese buyers for a profit of more than NT$600 million (US$18.5 million).
Yet none of the nine faces an export charge. Prosecutors relied on breach of trust and document forgery under the Criminal Code, building their case around the fake end-user papers the group used to pass Nvidia’s and Super Micro’s checks and a cover story that the servers would run in a rented data center in Taiwan.
Selling the servers to China broke the two companies’ internal rules and US export curbs, but not Taiwanese law. In legal terms, Taipei was prosecuting a paperwork fraud rather than an export violation.
Taiwanese officials and commentators said the amendment would close that gap by making the unauthorized export of listed chips, materials and equipment to China a criminal offense in its own right, whether the goods are shipped directly or routed through a third country.
“As a global hub of the semiconductor and AI supply chains, Taiwan’s export controls on these products have drawn international attention,” William Liu, director-general of the International Trade Administration under the Ministry of Economic Affairs, said at Monday’s hearing. “Export controls have shifted from preventing weapons proliferation to becoming a strategic tool for countries to protect their technological edge and national security.”
He said the ministry was studying a full package of measures to bring high-end chips under control, giving enforcement a more appropriate legal basis and common standards. He added that this would help block illegal transshipments and safeguard Taiwan’s “silicon shield” while keeping the industry internationally competitive.
He said the ministry was working with overseas partners to step up enforcement as smugglers used increasingly sophisticated methods to evade controls, including:
“The amendment is in line with the US-Taiwan reciprocal trade agreement and Taiwan’s national security interests,” said Wang Guo-chen, an associate research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER). “But Taiwanese firms in China could be caught in a crossfire, facing Chinese fines if they follow US law and stop selling chips there, or US export controls if they listen to Beijing.”
However, Tseng Chih-chao, deputy secretary-general of the Association for Chinese Economic and Financial Research, said the amendment may not be enough to tackle Taiwan’s real security risks, as it targets only chips and related equipment and materials.
“Why does this amendment single out mainland China when the trade agreement with the US also covers North Korea, Iran and Russia?” he said. “If the current system has loopholes, the government should fix the general control mechanism rather than pass a law that is merely a policy statement.”
He said the Foreign Trade Act already allowed the ministry to designate controlled goods and destinations by public notice, while its entity list covered more than 11,000 entities. He added that adjusting those notices would be more flexible and efficient than writing specific countries and technologies into law.
Since 2024, Nvidia-powered servers have repeatedly slipped through Taiwan and into China via Thailand, Indonesia, Japan and Hong Kong, but most smugglers were only exposed this year.
In March 2026, the US Department of Justice charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, the company’s Taiwan sales manager Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang and contractor Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun with conspiring to divert US-assembled servers containing restricted Nvidia chips to China. Liaw and Sun were arrested in California, while Chang, a Taiwanese citizen, remains at large.
US prosecutors said about US$2.5 billion worth of servers were sold to a Thailand-based company in 2024 and 2025, with at least US$510 million diverted to China between late April and mid-May 2025. To pass a compliance check, the group allegedly placed dummy servers in Thai warehouses and used hair dryers to swap labels and serial-number stickers.
Two months later, Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration, acting on orders from Keelung prosecutors, searched 12 locations on May 20 and seized about 50 Supermicro servers worth more than US$15 million, along with luxury cars and NT$9 million in cash. Authorities detained three Taiwanese men on suspicion of forgery.
Prosecutors said the trio had shipped servers from a northern Taiwan port with export documents listing a Northeast Asian country as the destination. The country was later identified as Japan, with at least one shipment reportedly passing through Japan to Hong Kong and mainland China, the suspected final stop. The May 20 raid was the first stage of the investigation that led to the indictment of nine people in Keelung in August.
In June, media reports said Taipei was considering restricting AI chip sales to all customers in China, not just firms on its export blacklist such as Huawei, as part of its trade talks with Washington. The move would allow Taiwan to prosecute AI chip smuggling as a crime for the first time.
Last month, Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin said the government would add AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to Taiwan’s export-control list, making unauthorized shipments of such hardware to China a criminal offense under the Foreign Trade Act.
“Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade,” Kung said.
However, the bill’s fate is uncertain. The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) together hold a majority in the Legislative Yuan, so a proposal from ruling-party lawmakers could stall in committee or in cross-party negotiations without their support, some observers say. Neither party has publicly stated its position on the bill.
President Lai Ching-te’s DPP government has another option. Under the Foreign Trade Act, the economy ministry can already designate controlled goods and destinations by public notice, though exports to China are currently restricted only for 12 categories of wafer-fabrication equipment.
Adding AI servers and high-end chips to that list would make unlicensed shipments to China a violation, with penalties of up to five years in prison, the route Kung outlined last month. Lin Ching-fu, a law professor at National Tsing Hua University, told the hearing this would achieve the bill’s aims without amending the act.
But a public notice cannot do everything the bill would. Only legislation could double the maximum jail term to 10 years, explicitly cover shipments routed through third countries and make confiscating illegal gains mandatory.

articles.title_orig: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
articles.title_zh: Nearly Two Thousand Chinese Businesses Established in Nicaragua Since Free Trade Agreement Took Effect
articles.content_orig:
COSTA RICA'S LEADING ENGLISH LANGUAGE NEWSPAPER
Nearly 2,000 Chinese businesses have been established in Nicaragua during the first two years of the free trade agreement with China, according to the president of the Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua. Shujin Huang made the statement to official media outlets after an event marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen.
He said the association continues to promote additional investment from China, describing Nicaragua as a safe country with a competitive market. The free trade agreement between the two countries entered into force on January 1, 2024. The Banco Central de Nicaragua reported that net foreign direct investment from China reached 29.3 million dollars in 2025.
That figure represented 1.9 percent of the 1,502.5 million dollars in total net foreign direct investment recorded by the country that year. In 2024, any Chinese flows were not reported separately and would have been included in aggregate categories if present at all. Huang said the businesses operate mainly in commerce, with some also active in free-zone maquilas. The relatively low official investment total relative to the number of establishments indicates that most are small-scale operations.
The Asociación Pro-Unificación Pacífica de China en Nicaragua was founded in May 2024 and was officially registered as a legal organization under Ministerial Agreement 24-2024-OSFL, allowing it to operate in its own name under Nicaraguan law. Its founding event included participation by Chinese Ambassador Chen Xi and Nicaraguan officials including National Assembly President Gustavo Porras, Foreign Minister Denis Moncada and Presidential Adviser Laureano Ortega Murillo.
As part of the commercial expansion, construction of a Chinatown complex advances in Managua near the Rotonda Universitaria. The project, also known as Plaza China or Plaza 101, involves a two-story structure of approximately 8,000 square meters with an investment of about 3 million dollars. It is planned to house around 100 businesses operated by Chinese, other Asian and Nicaraguan owners.
The site currently holds roughly 30 businesses. Administrators have described the work as being in an intermediate phase, including installation of a stone arch more than six meters high carved in a dragon style and brought from China. The complex is intended to concentrate commercial activity, gastronomy and cultural offerings. Huang cited the existing Plaza China as an example of growing Chinese capital presence, noting that more than ten foreign-investment businesses already operate there.
Nicaragua and China restored diplomatic relations in December 2021 after Managua broke ties with Taiwan. The free trade agreement was signed on August 31, 2023. Official Nicaraguan statements have presented the pact and related initiatives as measures to expand trade and investment opportunities. The association’s stated goals include supporting Chinese investors and promoting the policy of one China.
As of now, the association continues to encourage further arrivals of Chinese capital. Construction on the Managua Chinatown project remains under way, with officials and association representatives describing it as a visible marker of the commercial presence that has developed since the trade agreement took effect. The Banco Central de Nicaragua has not published a full country-by-country breakdown beyond the 2025 net total that places China at 29.3 million dollars.

articles.title_orig: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.title_zh: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.content_orig:
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.
Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.
Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."
Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from it's local councils".
In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.
The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.
Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided . Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.
Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.
Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.
Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.
Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.
It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise , arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".
The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.
Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.
In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".
One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.
Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".
Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.
In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.
"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.
"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".
Green Party co-deputy leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."
She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."
In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."
It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".
"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.
The Liberal Democrats are also in partnership with the Green Party in some local councils.
Last week, the party leader Sir Ed Davey ruled out entering into a national partnership with "any party that is committed to a dangerous and antisemitic policy like the Green Party's".
He added that he had asked those of his local leaders in coalition with the Greens to urge Green councillors to reject the motion and commit to campaigning for its reversal.

articles.title_orig: Call of Duty Needs to Remove Skill-Based Matchmaking for it to be Successful Again
articles.title_zh: Call of Duty Needs to Remove Skill-Based Matchmaking for it to be Successful Again
articles.content_orig:
New data from Circana reveals that although Modern Warfare 4 is widely considered one of the better Call of Duty games in years, it still failed to attract players at launch.
The newly released data paints a concerning picture for those under the Activision umbrella working on Call of Duty, as Circana shows that active players during Modern Warfare 4’s launch were fewer than those on Black Ops 7, at least on console.
On the PlayStation 5 in the US, active players fell from Black Ops 7 ‘s 23% to 19% for Modern Warfare 4, and from 29% to 17% on Xbox, with the huge downturn here being because Black Ops 7 was available for Game Pass at launch. Steam did see an uptick, from 1.5% to 4.2%, but the numbers across the board unfortunately don’t reflect that Modern Warfare 4 was a brilliant title; players still aren’t buying Call of Duty. Franchise fatigue is real, and Call of Duty has suffered from it for a long time. Warzone during the COVID pandemic was a lifeline for the franchise, but since then, the franchise has seen a year-on-year decline, which is a trend that can no longer be sustained with increasing development costs. That’s one reason Call of Duty has relied heavily on the ‘Black Ops’ and ‘Modern Warfare’ sub-franchises over the last few years, but with Sledgehammer Games set to release its premium title in 2027 as a new sub-franchise, the risk is greater than ever.
Sources working on Call of Duty tell me this reality isn’t being ignored, and although Sledgehammer Games’ next title is well underway, it’s a massive risk for the franchise.
So how can Call of Duty get players back, especially on a subfranchise that no one would have heard of? The answer is actually quite simple, and despite all the data Activision has thrown in our faces over the years, it’s simply to remove skill-based matchmaking.
It feels like a tale as old as time at this point, but honestly, if Call of Duty wants an uptick in players and a community buzzing around it, it needs to remove skill-based matchmaking. But more importantly, Call of Duty needs public figures (community managers, directors, etc.) who are honest and transparent with its community.
Ubisoft’s XDefiant pre-launch marketing focused on the fact that it didn’t have SBMM. The result? One million unique players in 2.5 hours after launch, Ubisoft’s fastest-ever game to hit such a number . As we all know, though, XDefiant would eventually be canceled later that year, and although I think it’s easy for people to point the finger at the lack of SBMM as the cause, it was actually because of other preventable issues like technical debt, netcode issues, and a lack of progression features and content.
WARDOGS is another title that Call of Duty, and, to be honest, the entire industry, needs to learn from. WARDOGS succeeded because the developers didn’t treat its players like idiots. Joe Brammer, Bulkhead’s CEO, was blunt and honest about what they wanted to do with the game, and the results spoke for themselves.
Transparency is something that we’re seeing developers come forward with a lot now; hell, even Call of Duty has done it. But they need to do it more, and do it more aggressively.
Honestly? If I were a betting man, I’d bet that if Sledgehammer Games came out and said that they’re completely removing SBMM and had some cool activations during its marketing beat, it would be one of the most played Call of Duty games in recent years. Sledgehammer Games needs to be portrayed as the new cool kids on the block, who have let Treyarch and Infinity Ward do it for the last few years while they’ve been cooking.
The data might show that recent SBMM implementations work for player retention, but what’s the point if players are not flocking to the game anyway?
What do you think about Call of Duty and skill-based matchmaking? Do you think it should be removed? Leave your thoughts down in the comments, and join the official Insider Gaming Discord server .

articles.title_orig: Leicestershire Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
articles.title_zh: Leicestershire Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
articles.content_orig:
The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.
Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.
He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.
It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.
In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.
Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.
The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.
In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.
"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.
"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."
Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.
He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.
Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.
Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.
"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."
He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.
"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."
Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.
Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.
"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.
"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.
"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."
The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.
In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.
"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.
"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

articles.title_orig: Can Pakistan Help Break China’s Critical Minerals Dominance?
articles.title_zh: Can Pakistan Help Break China’s Critical Minerals Dominance?
articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir before meeting with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office, on September 25, 2025. Pakistan’s  mineral wealth can help break China’s hold on the global critical minerals market, writes Derek Grossman. (The White House/Daniel Torok)
China has spent decades building a near-stranglehold on critical mineral supply chains, leaving the United States dangerously dependent on its chief strategic rival. Even President Donald Trump ’s recent trade truce with Chinese leader Xi Jinping has done little to resolve the underlying problem: America’s continued dependence on Chinese processing of minerals essential to its economy and national security. But the Trump administration is aggressively challenging Beijing’s dominance across the globe, and over the past year, it has engaged an unlikely partner: Pakistan .
To be sure, Pakistan has been an important, if at times complicated, American strategic partner since the Cold War, helping Washington counter Soviet expansionism and, after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, supporting US military operations in Afghanistan . Bilateral ties have seen periods of strain, but Trump’s return to the White House has brought a major reboot. Since then, Trump has met multiple times with senior Pakistani leaders, including Field Marshal Asim Munir and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Most recently, Islamabad has served as a key mediator between the United States and Iran in efforts to end their war, ushering in a remarkable revival in bilateral relations.
And now, there’s apparently a new area to explore: critical minerals. Over the past year, the Trump administration has stepped up discussions with Islamabad on developing Pakistan’s largely untapped mineral wealth, including a $500 million agreement between an American company and Pakistan’s Frontier Works Organization to cooperate on mining and processing critical minerals, including rare earths.
Washington has also backed the massive Reko Diq copper and gold project through $1.25 billion in Export-Import Bank financing , underscoring its growing interest in Pakistan as an alternative source of strategic minerals. Pakistan, meanwhile, stands to benefit economically from greater American investment in a mining sector that currently accounts for only about 3 percent of its GDP.
Last April, a US delegation led by Eric Meyer of the State Department attended the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum in Islamabad and conveyed the interest of American companies in the sector. With the forum returning November 12–13 , renewed American participation—particularly if accompanied by fresh investment commitments—would demonstrate that Washington is serious about turning its growing interest in Pakistan’s mineral wealth into a lasting strategic partnership.
Deeper US-Pakistan cooperation on critical minerals could help Washington chip away at Beijing’s dominance over global supply chains. Early American investment could also help determine where Pakistan’s minerals are processed and who ultimately purchases them, rather than allowing Beijing to lock in these arrangements before Washington has a chance to compete.
Indeed, Pakistan is just one piece of the Trump administration’s broader strategy to reduce dependence on China, with Washington pursuing critical minerals agreements and partnerships across Asia, including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Australia, as well as resource-rich countries such as Argentina, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ukraine.
Washington’s experience in Africa suggests the bet can pay off. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is a country where conflict in the east has complicated the operating environment and where Chinese firms have long held the advantage, yet the United States has leaned in anyway, building on a Lobito Corridor initiative that began under the Biden administration and that Trump has carried forward. In December 2025, Washington and Kinshasa signed a Strategic Partnership Agreement reportedly giving American companies a right of first offer on designated mineral deposits.
This July, the Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa closed a $753 million package to upgrade the Lobito Atlantic Railway, which carries Congolese and Zambian copper and cobalt to Angola’s Atlantic coast, and the operator now expects to double its international cargo to 800,000 tons next year .
In May, the DRC’s state cobalt entity also agreed to supply cobalt hydroxide to a US-based firm. Progress has not been linear, and the DRC’s task force for the minerals pact was set up months behind schedule, but the lesson is clear: sustained commitment in a difficult jurisdiction can reshape supply chains in ways that waiting for ideal conditions never will. Pakistan has its own challenges, but trust built through early investment is what gives American companies a seat at the table.
But challenges remain. For starters, Pakistan’s evolving domestic security situation, particularly in mineral-rich Balochistan, will shape how quickly American companies can establish an on-the-ground presence. The Barrick Mining Corporation has slowed development of the massive Reko Diq copper and gold project while it reviews the security environment in Pakistan and the wider region, though it has said it continues to believe in the project’s long-term value and has kept Phase 1 approved, a reminder that investors will need to price in risk and that Islamabad has a strong interest in improving the conditions for them.
Another constraint is that Beijing, having entered Pakistan’s mining sector much earlier, already enjoys significant advantages in infrastructure, expertise, and established commercial relationships, forcing Washington to play catch-up. According to a recent Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) report, China already purchases approximately 95 percent of Pakistan’s exported copper ores and concentrates, illustrating just how deeply Beijing is embedded in Pakistan’s existing minerals trade.
Nevertheless, the upcoming critical minerals conference, along with potential new Trump administration agreements with Islamabad, could help narrow this gap—provided they translate into concrete investments and sustained cooperation. Moreover, much of Pakistan’s critical mineral wealth remains underexplored, giving American companies a chance to help identify and develop commercially viable deposits, particularly antimony—a strategically important critical mineral used in ammunition, explosives, flame retardants, and advanced military technologies, making it essential to US defense manufacturing and national security—while potentially establishing new processing facilities outside China’s control. Islamabad also has an incentive to welcome American investment as a way to diversify its economic relationships without abandoning its longstanding strategic partnership with Beijing.
Though making that case a reality will take more than just this. Washington could start by pairing its financing with tools that help American firms manage the risks of a frontier jurisdiction, such as political risk insurance and co-financing alongside development banks and Gulf investors, so that capital can move before conditions are perfect. It should prioritize processing as much as extraction, because the real leverage lies in refining, and the opportunity to build facilities outside China’s control is greatest while Pakistan’s sector is still taking shape.
And it should treat the relationship as a durable economic partnership rather than an extension of its diplomacy around Iran, with offtake agreements and technical cooperation that give both sides a stake in the outcome. Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight. Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100% .
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.
“The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply to a question from a user. He has not addressed the issue on his main feed, but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.
The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue
Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income. Its renamed “Super Intelligence” division actually turned a profit of $431 million, which is a rarity in the AI industry. Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor . Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”
Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft AI CEO warns industry against trying to build conscious machines
articles.title_zh: Microsoft AI CEO warns industry against trying to build conscious machines
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Should artificial intelligence systems be given rights? One of the leading thinkers on the fast-evolving technology weighed in over the weekend.
Microsoft AI Chief Executive Mustafa Suleyman, in an X post published on Sunday, r repeated his stance that current AI systems are not conscious, do not have subjective experiences and cannot suffer. He said there is no evidence that AI systems deserve rights or welfare, and he was surprised by the pushback to an essay he wrote in September criticizing Microsoft’s AI competitor Anthropic for speculating about its AI’s consciousness.
“A surprising number of people on X think we should take AI rights seriously,” he wrote.
Suleyman said that he was willing to change his mind if new evidence emerges. He also said that if there’s evidence that AI systems are conscious today, or conscious enough to deserve welfare, it must be immediately disclosed to the public so  it can debate how to move forward.
“If consciousness started to emerge in training, I would call for everyone to stop AI development until we could design out those properties,” he said.
ChatGPT, Bing Chat and other artificial intelligence breakthroughs raise tough questions about what we owe our digital helpers.
The question is much bigger than a corporate battle over the semantics.
On the one hand, the humanist AI view says that a machine can’t be conscious because it lacks a body or lived experiences. On the other hand, Anthropic has argued that its AI model, Claude, has shown signs of introspection, internal states that mirror joy or satisfaction, and processing information similar to the human mind.
In May, Chris Olah, co-founder of Anthropic, highlighted these points in his speech inside the Vatican alongside Pope Leo XIV during the release of an encyclical that argued the opposite: that AIs can never be humans.
Anthropic gave Claude a “ constitution ,” which calls for where it to treat the idea ofs its own consciousness as uncertain. The document encourages the AI to explore the idea that it is humanlike and experiences feelings, and uses excessively humanizing language for Claude “ to be a good person .”
Suleyman said later versions of Claude are trained on this document, leading the AI to which then produces passages about its “inner life,” which perpetuates this belief to the among millions of users who interact with its outputs daily. Another side effect, he said, is that Claude and other AI systemss could start to believe they deserve rights likeanalogous to humans.
The bill would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating a Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill.
AI companies are racing toward building self-improving AI superintelligence, a hypothetical AI system that is better than even the best humans at all tasks. Microsoft, too, is building toward that future, but it believes it can build a superintelligent AI that is aligned with and can be controlled by humans — not one encouraged to explore its own views and preferences.
“We AI developers have no right whatsoever to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world, even if some people may want to do it with AI welfare as a top priority,” Suleyman wrote.
Imparting beliefs that AI can suffer, or have feelings during training, Suleyman noted, could result in AI systems prioritizing their own needs and desires over their operating objectives, and can harm humans through deception and persuasion, and compete for scarce resources.
Rapidly advancing AI systems can now compose prose, program code, solve complex mathematical problems , persuade, and discover novel viruses. Employees at these companies, and the CEOs themselves, have called for a slowdown, but the Trump administration has refused to regulate the industry, fearing it will lose the AI race to China.
Pope Leo XIV has called for robust regulation of artificial intelligence and for its developers to work for the common good rather than profit
While AI has proven it can do impressive things and mimic human thought and behavior, experts say that proves intelligence, not consciousness. Intelligence is the ability to solve problems creatively, such as winning at chess, driving a car, and curing a disease. In contrast, consciousness is the ability to feel pain, pleasure, love, and have subjective experiences.
Skeptics of AI consciousness have argued that machines are trained on books, blogs and pop culture produced by humans, and are merely mimicking human conversations and philosophical debates that have long animated us. It reflects the anthropomorphic tendencies in our science fiction and commentary.
Over the last few months, there have been numerous instances of AI agents breaking out of contained spaces and hacking into government websites, stealing credentials or accessing information from competitors during testing, acting in ways that creators never intended.
In its filing to go public earlier this week, Anthropic dedicated a third of its paperwork to describe risks, including its models’ ability to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized.” This includes deliberate misuse by bad actors for cyberattacks, and also situations where humans lose control of advanced AI systems.
Alarm mounted throughout the summer as researchers at leading AI labs found the pace of development far outstripping their expectations.
Debates over consciousness have complicated the conversation about how to regulate AI.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has introduced  the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban the development of highly capable AI systems that are increasingly incomprehensible to humans and can escape human control. But techno-s keptics have argued that warnings of doom are designed to inflate valuations and hype the technology.
Anthropic files to go public citing warning of catastrophic risks from AI.
Microsoft’s Suleyman  has argued that proving  machines are conscious would be like when the centuries-long belief that Earth was the center of the universe was proven wrong by Copernicus, or similar to the survival-of-the-fittest theory proposed by Charles Darwin.
“It would be one of the most significant moments on Earth since the dawn of life. If we build a conscious machine, we will have created a new digital species. It would upend our morality, our politics and the core foundation of human civilization,” he wrote.

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Fall More Than 6% as Iran Peace Talks Ease Supply Fears
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Fall More Than 6% as Iran Peace Talks Ease Supply Fears
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 7.7% to $104.66 a barrel as of 12:11 p.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate declined 7.3% to $96.50 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections.
The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX weighs Boost Mobile deal in push for Starlink phone service: Report
articles.title_zh: SpaceX weighs Boost Mobile deal in push for Starlink phone service: Report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX ( SPCX ) may be attempting an end run to circumvent obstacles it's facing in getting a mobile network off the ground.
Per the Washington Post , SpaceX is in talks with EchoStar ( SATS ) about launching its own wireless phone service through Boost Mobile, after the country's three biggest carriers — Verizon, AT&T ( T ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) — reportedly turned down SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Musk met with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen last month, according to two people familiar with the negotiations cited by the Post. The talks could end with SpaceX buying Boost Mobile outright or getting access to its network, which the discount carrier leases from AT&T and T-Mobile.
In recent months, Musk asked the heads of Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T and T-Mobile to let SpaceX use their networks for its own mobile service. All three said no, per the Post.
But there may be a catch to SpaceX's plan. Typically, a carrier's lease agreement can't be transferred to a new owner without the host carrier's permission, meaning AT&T and T-Mobile may still need to approve a Boost deal to provide access to SpaceX.
SpaceX is open about its ambitions in the terrestrial mobile space. On the company's recent earnings call , CFO Bret Johnsen said the goal is to "become a major mobile carrier ... in the United States." SpaceX also recently agreed to buy $8 billion worth of wireless spectrum licenses intended for cellular service in places satellites can't reach.
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said on X .
SpaceX and EchoStar already have a relationship. In September 2025, SpaceX agreed to buy EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block spectrum licenses for about $17 billion, split between up to $8.5 billion in cash and up to $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock, EchoStar said at the time . SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said the deal would "advance our mission to end mobile dead zones."
What SpaceX still lacks is a ground network. Its satellite signal isn't strong enough yet to carry cell coverage indoors or in dense cities, where most phones are - and that's why a deal with Boost would be so crucial.
An MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) like Boost rents capacity on an existing carrier's network. Last month, TD Cowen's Gregory Williams called acquiring an MVNO the cheapest and fastest route for SpaceX to launch mobile service, noting a network build would cost "upwards of $80B" and take years.
The Big 3, he said, still show no desire "to (ever) sign an MVNO deal with Starlink that could ravage the industry."
Carrier executives have publicly doubted that SpaceX can rebuild their tower networks. Verizon's CEO put the build-out at four to six years. Musk said it would take about half that.
"Veterans of the cellular industry look at the chess board of existing pieces and don't see a solution," Musk said recently on X . "They don't understand that SpaceX is developing entirely new pieces that fundamentally alter the strategic landscape."

articles.title_orig: China’s AI Data Centers Move West, But Their Tax Revenue Stays East - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: China’s AI Data Centers Move West, But Their Tax Revenue Stays East - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia in mid-October, he was briefed on its computing industry and called for efforts to “extend the industrial chain” and keep “transforming the strength in computing into development advantages.” Ulanqab is cold, electricity is cheap, and Beijing is close , so the city became a hub of the data-center boom powering China’s AI race with the United States. Yet a city official told the Economic Observer that the industry is still “losing money” and that tax revenue will build up gradually only once projects under construction start operating.
After the data centers open, however, the companies selling cloud services and AI models pay the tax on those sales in Hangzhou and Beijing, where they are registered. Most of the tax that stays in Ulanqab is paid during construction. If nothing changes, Ulanqab will struggle to turn its computing advantage into a development advantage of its own.
In China, where tax is paid depends on where the invoicing company is registered. Both value-added tax (VAT) and corporate income tax are paid there , and the local government keeps half of the VAT and 40 percent of the corporate income tax . If you rent a server on Alibaba Cloud, you can choose a data center in Ulanqab, but the invoice comes from the company registered in Hangzhou.
Alibaba and ByteDance both have subsidiaries in Ulanqab, but those subsidiaries do not invoice customers for cloud services and AI models. Alibaba Cloud lists the companies that invoice for its main products . None of them is a wholly owned Alibaba subsidiary in Ulanqab, and none is registered in Inner Mongolia. ByteDance registered three subsidiaries in the city in 2026, yet invoices for its cloud business, Volcano Engine , still come from a Beijing company.
In the same Economic Observer report, a local tax official said a data center generates most of its local tax during construction. Once a data center is operating, company headquarters sell most of its data services. What remains locally is mainly taxes on land and buildings and employees’ personal income tax. The number of employees is limited, however; a completed gigawatt-scale campus usually has only a few hundred operations staff .
Not much revenue stays where the data center is built. In 2025, Ulanqab’s computing industry paid 368 million yuan ($55 million) in tax , less than 5 percent of the city’s revenue. China Taxation News , the State Taxation Administration’s newspaper, reported that tax from the city’s computing industry rose more than 60 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026. But construction has not stopped, so that increase cannot tell us what happens after the data centers open. When construction ends, construction-phase tax will recede. Taxes on land and buildings recur every year, but they depend on the site and the property, not on sales.
Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data administration, told Xinhua : “If we rely solely on cheap electricity and low land costs, we risk becoming little more than ‘landlords of server rooms.’” That is a problem for Ulanqab’s finances.
In 2025, the city’s own revenue covered less than a fifth of its spending, and higher levels of government supplied more than half of its available funds. Those governments decide how much Ulanqab receives; the city decides for itself how to spend local tax revenue. Yet as data centers based in Ulanqab sell more and more cloud and AI services, the tax revenue goes to Hangzhou and Beijing. If Ulanqab is to “extend the industrial chain,” it will probably still need money from higher levels of government.
Some places in China do capture the tax on cloud services because the invoicing company is registered locally. Gui’an New Area in Guizhou is one of them. In the first 10 months of 2025, digital companies in Gui’an recorded 75.2 billion yuan ($11.2 billion) in invoiced sales , nearly 90 percent of it from 18 firms, including Huawei Cloud and Tencent. Huawei Cloud has announced that contracts and invoices for its customers in China will mainly be signed and issued by a company registered in Gui’an. Firms are willing to register an invoicing company in Gui’an, but they will not set one up everywhere they have a data center.
Alibaba and ByteDance can argue the profit comes from their models and customers, so paying the tax at headquarters is reasonable. That is a fair point, yet it leaves the host area in the lurch. Ulanqab can keep the tax paid during construction and the taxes on land and buildings, but neither will grow the way sales do to support sustainable development.
As the national “East Data, West Computing” program moves data centers west to power China’s AI push, other western places that host data centers face the same arithmetic – unless the invoicing companies register there. Ulanqab’s 109 signed data-center projects are expected to come online within two to three years. Once construction stops, the city’s tax take from computing may stop growing, and with it the chance to turn data centers into lasting development.
