articles.title_orig: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.title_zh: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.content_orig:
Watch: What we know so far about the fake emergency alerts in Russia and Ukraine
Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected.
Regular alerts warn Ukrainians to take shelter from incoming attacks but the system was compromised on Sunday (file photo)
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether.
After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels.
In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel."
The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised".
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'.
"I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack."
Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian.
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
A Ukrainian government agency published translated versions of some of the fake alerts
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets.
Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks.
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."
Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."
The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Oil prices extended losses from Asian trade into early Monday morning U.S. time as a draft proposal on a potential end to the U.S.-Iran war is now being circulated after Iranian negotiators left Qatar, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters on Monday.
Oil prices slumped by 3% in Asian trade on Monday amid renewed optimism about a possible peace deal between the United States and Iran, following reports about mediation talks between Iran and Qatar over the weekend.
Iranian negotiators left Qatar on Sunday and a draft proposal is now being circulated for a potential follow-up meeting, the Reuters source said, without elaborating on what the draft proposal could possibly entail.
“Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now,” KCM Trade’s chief market analyst Tim Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters earlier today.
“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently,” Reuters quoted Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, as saying.
“These demands are reasonable and logical: no final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought ‌to an end, Iran's demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” the Iranian official said.
Iran this weekend said that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within two days if its demands are met, faster than the week for reopening Tehran had aired in September.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s September proposal.
“It remains to be seen whether this will lead to anything,” ING’s commodities analysts Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said in a Monday note, commenting on the Iran-Qatar mediation talks.
Early on Monday, Brent Crude prices had dropped to $108.61, per barrel, down by 4.25% on the day, and WTI Crude slumped by 4.32% to below $100 a barrel, at $99.62.
Still, the market is apprehensive that new U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran could follow the U.S. midterm elections.
“Given that many of the key developments in this conflict have unfolded over weekends, the market may have to hold its breath until the end of the week,” ING’s strategists said.

articles.title_orig: How would Tehran respond if the US and Israel bomb Iran again?
articles.title_zh: How would Tehran respond if the US and Israel bomb Iran again?
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s military is warning that if all-out war breaks out again with the United States and Israel, it will be longer and more costly than their rivals expect.
Iran’s armed forces could deploy new weapons and tactics against the US, Israel and other countries, which would be the third major conflict between the countries since June last year.
There have been increasing signs that the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which began on February 28, could restart after the US midterm elections. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the war with Iran will end “very soon one way or the other” and Tehran should agree a deal or “the hammer” will come down.
Hossein Kanani Moghaddam, a former senior IRGC commander, told Al Jazeera that despite extensive blows to the Iranian armed forces during US and Israeli strikes earlier this year, they are now in better operational shape compared with previous conflicts.
“In terms of offence, our target database has significantly expanded, the range, accuracy and warheads of our missiles have improved and our drone capabilities have increased,” he said.
New enemy assets were being identified and operations in additional geographical areas were being planned, he added. Arkaminia said that previously undisclosed capabilities and targets would be revealed – and used – if Iran is attacked again.
Commanders from Iran’s General Staff of Armed Forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Islamic Republic of Iran Army are reported to have recently met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to discuss what steps will be taken if attacked again. The response will be immediate and could go beyond the West Asia region , they said.
The IRGC was “100 percent ready” to confront another attack, spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said on Sunday evening, describing “maximum deterrence” as a goal Iran would reach in the near future.
Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said the commanders would rely on “asymmetric warfare” tactics that would compensate for the superiority of US military equipment.
He added that “some weaponry was renovated and new equipment was added along with new tactics” during the brief ceasefire period that came after the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US.
Last month, state television showed an underground drone production line. The authorities also showcased an upgraded version of the Arash attack drone and claimed that its warhead had doubled to 100kg with improved guidance.
According to a Reuters investigation published last week, numerous military agencies linked with Iran’s defence establishment have evaded sanctions and funnelled billions into military imports to replenish the IRGC. The imports between January 2025 and June this year from China, Russia and Germany to fuel missile and drone production included rocket propellants, explosives, detonators, titanium and heavy-duty trucks that could be used as launchers.
Many Iranian missile defence systems, radars and other equipment were hit during the war. But Kanani Moghaddam said remaining and newly developed systems were becoming more accurate, pointing to the targeting of a US-built F-35 and other warplanes and drones as successes that can be replicated and expanded upon.
“At sea, we have shown that we can easily target supertankers,” he said regarding transit through the Strait of Hormuz that is deemed “unauthorised” by Iranian authorities. He said Iranian attacks on US Navy vessels in September prompted them to stop venturing into the critical waterway since. But the US has continued its naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, while Iran’s civilian population and infrastructure remain largely exposed if the war resumes.
Tehran and other cities across the country lack shelters or early warning systems to protect civilians. Authorities have not reported any progress regarding the promised shelters and gaps in public warning arrangements.
Iran’s electricity grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, petrochemical and steel manufacturers and roads and railways could also be attacked again, making life even more difficult amid the economic crisis.
During both wars, many senior political and military figures of the Islamic Republic were killed by US and Israeli strikes.
The new supreme leader has not been seen or heard from since replacing his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in early March, ostensibly for security reasons.
This has led to tighter domestic security controls, and prompted some voices from within the establishment to raise concerns and demand accountability for intelligence failures and protection of leadership.
“We have been hit and hit hard,” state-linked analyst Hamzeh Rahim Safavi said during a televised debate on Saturday. “The main cause is intelligence weakness, but no one talks about it or is held accountable”.
The analyst is the son of Yahya Rahim Safavi, a former commander-in-chief of the IRGC who currently serves as a senior military adviser to the supreme leader. The analyst said calls by hardliners to acquire a nuclear bomb would not repair intelligence and security weaknesses.
But Esmaeil Kowsari, a former IRGC division commander now a parliamentary national-security commission member, told local media last week that even though the supreme leader and others were assassinated, “the enemies did not reach their main goals”. He said the goals were to overthrow the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran.
“On the eve of their elections, the Americans are trying to pretend that they have achieved victory by causing a ruckus and launching psychological operations, but that is not the truth,” Kowsari said.

articles.title_orig: Inside Apple’s Slog to Create Its First Robot
articles.title_zh: Inside Apple’s Slog to Create Its First Robot
articles.content_orig:
Breaking News Apple’s robotics ambitions reportedly stretch far beyond the more advanced HomeView currently in development, with the company having explored machines that could follow users around the home, fly indoors, and even fold clothes.
According to The Information , Apple has investigated several different home-robot concepts as part of a wider push into robotics. There is no indication that all, or even any, of these experimental devices will eventually be released.
The ideas reportedly include a wheeled robot capable of following a person from room to room, a device designed to fly inside the home, and another concept intended to fold clothes.
The concept closest to becoming a real product is Apple’s higher-end robotic HomeView. The Apple Post previously reported that Apple is developing a roughly 9-inch HomeView mounted on a motorized 360-degree arm , with the screen able to turn toward whoever is speaking.
The latest report adds that the device could use cameras and sensors to understand its surroundings and act autonomously. The current HomeView already serves as the center of Apple’s expanding smart home ecosystem , combining Siri AI, FaceTime, media playback and Apple Home controls.
Apple has also been experimenting with sensors and visual intelligence across its home hardware. Earlier software references pointed to unreleased home accessories with cameras, sensors and visual-reasoning capabilities .
The various concepts suggest Apple is exploring ways to move Apple Intelligence beyond screens and speakers into devices that can physically react to their environment.
A robot that follows a user could theoretically keep FaceTime, Siri or smart home controls nearby as someone moves between rooms. A flying device or clothes-folding robot would represent a much more ambitious leap into general-purpose home robotics.
For now, those ideas remain experiments. The Information does not say that Apple has committed to releasing the wheeled, flying or clothes-folding concepts, and large technology companies routinely test hardware that never reaches customers.
Apple’s immediate smart home focus remains HomeView, which was officially unveiled in October and launches November 13. The rumored robotic HomeView is reportedly targeted for 2027, although it could slip into 2028.

articles.title_orig: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
articles.title_zh: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
articles.content_orig:
Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled more than 6% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.267%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 296, up 270% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.
While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Where things stand on Iran after tense weekend as its delegation has left Qatar
articles.title_zh: Where things stand on Iran after tense weekend as its delegation has left Qatar
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s military is warning that if all-out war breaks out again with the United States and Israel, it will be longer and more costly than their rivals expect.
Iran’s armed forces could deploy new weapons and tactics against the US, Israel and other countries, which would be the third major conflict between the countries since June last year.
There have been increasing signs that the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which began on February 28, could restart after the US midterm elections. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the war with Iran will end “very soon one way or the other” and Tehran should agree a deal or “the hammer” will come down.
Hossein Kanani Moghaddam, a former senior IRGC commander, told Al Jazeera that despite extensive blows to the Iranian armed forces during US and Israeli strikes earlier this year, they are now in better operational shape compared with previous conflicts.
“In terms of offence, our target database has significantly expanded, the range, accuracy and warheads of our missiles have improved and our drone capabilities have increased,” he said.
New enemy assets were being identified and operations in additional geographical areas were being planned, he added. Arkaminia said that previously undisclosed capabilities and targets would be revealed – and used – if Iran is attacked again.
Commanders from Iran’s General Staff of Armed Forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Islamic Republic of Iran Army are reported to have recently met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to discuss what steps will be taken if attacked again. The response will be immediate and could go beyond the West Asia region , they said.
The IRGC was “100 percent ready” to confront another attack, spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said on Sunday evening, describing “maximum deterrence” as a goal Iran would reach in the near future.
Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said the commanders would rely on “asymmetric warfare” tactics that would compensate for the superiority of US military equipment.
He added that “some weaponry was renovated and new equipment was added along with new tactics” during the brief ceasefire period that came after the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US.
Last month, state television showed an underground drone production line. The authorities also showcased an upgraded version of the Arash attack drone and claimed that its warhead had doubled to 100kg with improved guidance.
According to a Reuters investigation published last week, numerous military agencies linked with Iran’s defence establishment have evaded sanctions and funnelled billions into military imports to replenish the IRGC. The imports between January 2025 and June this year from China, Russia and Germany to fuel missile and drone production included rocket propellants, explosives, detonators, titanium and heavy-duty trucks that could be used as launchers.
Many Iranian missile defence systems, radars and other equipment were hit during the war. But Kanani Moghaddam said remaining and newly developed systems were becoming more accurate, pointing to the targeting of a US-built F-35 and other warplanes and drones as successes that can be replicated and expanded upon.
“At sea, we have shown that we can easily target supertankers,” he said regarding transit through the Strait of Hormuz that is deemed “unauthorised” by Iranian authorities. He said Iranian attacks on US Navy vessels in September prompted them to stop venturing into the critical waterway since. But the US has continued its naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, while Iran’s civilian population and infrastructure remain largely exposed if the war resumes.
Tehran and other cities across the country lack shelters or early warning systems to protect civilians. Authorities have not reported any progress regarding the promised shelters and gaps in public warning arrangements.
Iran’s electricity grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, petrochemical and steel manufacturers and roads and railways could also be attacked again, making life even more difficult amid the economic crisis.
During both wars, many senior political and military figures of the Islamic Republic were killed by US and Israeli strikes.
The new supreme leader has not been seen or heard from since replacing his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in early March, ostensibly for security reasons.
This has led to tighter domestic security controls, and prompted some voices from within the establishment to raise concerns and demand accountability for intelligence failures and protection of leadership.
“We have been hit and hit hard,” state-linked analyst Hamzeh Rahim Safavi said during a televised debate on Saturday. “The main cause is intelligence weakness, but no one talks about it or is held accountable”.
The analyst is the son of Yahya Rahim Safavi, a former commander-in-chief of the IRGC who currently serves as a senior military adviser to the supreme leader. The analyst said calls by hardliners to acquire a nuclear bomb would not repair intelligence and security weaknesses.
But Esmaeil Kowsari, a former IRGC division commander now a parliamentary national-security commission member, told local media last week that even though the supreme leader and others were assassinated, “the enemies did not reach their main goals”. He said the goals were to overthrow the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran.
“On the eve of their elections, the Americans are trying to pretend that they have achieved victory by causing a ruckus and launching psychological operations, but that is not the truth,” Kowsari said.

articles.title_orig: Goodbye to the toilet brush: the more hygienic alternative more and more bathrooms are switching to
articles.title_zh: Goodbye to the toilet brush: the more hygienic alternative more and more bathrooms are switching to
articles.content_orig:
TheCoolist is a mood board for your headspace.
It sits next to every toilet, usually in a closed holder, and a Finnish cleaning expert says many people keep it far too long. In Scandinavia and Central Europe, home sites report that many households are now swapping the classic bristle toilet brush for a different design. Here’s what is replacing it, why cleaning pros say it’s more hygienic, and what it still can’t do.
According to the Norwegian site Dagens.no , many people are choosing a silicone brush over the traditional plastic one. The reasons it gives: there are no dense bristles for dirt to collect in, so the head rinses clean; the flexible head reaches the edges and hard-to-access areas; it tends to spray less; and it is often sold with a ventilated or wall-mounted holder that lets it dry faster. The site quotes Finnish cleaning expert Mari Breilin, who says plastic brushes should be replaced considerably more often than many people do. The price, it adds, is about the same as many ordinary brushes.
The British testing site Expert Reviews sums it up: bristles are “so tightly packed together that it’s impossible to clean them perfectly,” so “bacteria build-up on the brush is inevitable,” and they “need replacing much more often.” Cleaning expert Isabella Flores, of Sparkly Maid San Diego, told Tom’s Guide that silicone is non-porous, so it doesn’t absorb bacteria and organic matter the way plastic bristles can. It also dries faster and tolerates harsher disinfection, including boiling.
Silicone or not, the routine is what keeps it hygienic. Tom’s Guide recommends:
Silicone is not a miracle. Expert Reviews notes that silicone brushes shaped like regular ones “usually have weak bristles that don’t do a great job on stubborn dirt,” and that flat, spatula-style heads handle grime better, though you have to get used to a different technique. And no brush, silicone or bristle, is built to dissolve the hard mineral ring at the waterline. And whatever you choose, a brush kept damp in a closed holder will still breed bacteria.
For that waterline ring, here’s the best way to remove limescale from the toilet . The bathroom is changing in other ways too, like the option replacing toilet paper , and the floor around the base deserves attention: see why people are spraying vinegar around the toilet .
A flat silicone head, an open holder and a date to replace it. That’s the trick.

articles.title_orig: Trump's Iran threat renews Gulf fears of a war it didn't choose
articles.title_zh: Trump's Iran threat renews Gulf fears of a war it didn't choose
articles.content_orig:
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title_orig: Why investors are dumping tech stocks, in one image
articles.title_zh: Why investors are dumping tech stocks, in one image
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Tech stocks aren't getting shredded for any old reason. It's actually very fundamental: Free cash flow is drying up for Big Tech leaders, and capex is rising dramatically.
Investors are questioning whether this ratio is totally out of whack, given more realistic growth projections for AI.
The combined capex of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft rose by $36.9 billion in the third quarter to $201.9 billion, the team at The Kobeissi Letter calculated (chart below). This figure has more than doubled over the past 12 months, and is up a staggering 356% since the first quarter of 2024.
Big Tech has now spent $1.6 trillion on capex over the last three years, the strategists say. At the same time, the combined free cash flow of these companies fell $33.1 billion last quarter to a negative $26.4 billion, its lowest on record. Free cash flow among these tech beasts has fallen by $88.2 billion over the last year. Only Microsoft reported positive free cash flow in the third quarter. Looking ahead, the strategists estimate these four companies plan to spend another $232 billion on capex in the fourth quarter.
The AI trade saw a serious slamming on Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about the weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech.
"The AI narrative is cracking as profitability concerns intensify," warned Miller Tabak chief markets strategist Matt Maley.

articles.title_orig: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap
articles.title_zh: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap
articles.content_orig:
The China Mono Premium, the OPIS assessment for mono-grade polysilicon used in n-type ingot production, was unchanged at CNY 38.786 ($5.82)/kg, or CNY 0.081/W, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Oct. 27.
According to market participants, the fundamentals of the Chinese polysilicon market remain unchanged, with the market continuing to be characterized by manufacturers holding firm to full-cost-based offers while downstream buyers show limited willingness to accept current prices. This has kept prices largely at a standstill, with inventory levels exceeding 500,000 metric tons (MT) further prolonging the impasse.
Industry participants widely noted that futures prices, which remain significantly below mainstream spot prices, have provided a degree of balance to the ongoing standoff between upstream suppliers and downstream buyers. According to data from the Guangzhou Futures Exchange on Oct. 26, settlement prices for polysilicon futures contracts for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027 ranged from a low of CNY 33.620/kg to a high of CNY 37.180/kg, with even the highest about 4.14% below the latest spot assessment.
Market participants explained that actual spot transactions continue to be concluded at higher prices than futures contracts, partly because customers with long-term purchase agreements still need to procure some material in the spot market. To offset the higher procurement costs, these buyers also source relatively lower-priced polysilicon from futures traders, helping to balance their overall purchasing costs.
One trade participant said that futures traders had been gradually selling off previously accumulated stocks of low-priced polysilicon into the spot market. However, the availability of this lower-priced material is expected to diminish over time. The participant added that manufacturers adhering to the industry self-discipline agreement appear determined not to sell polysilicon at prices below CNY 40/kg during the fourth quarter. As low-priced supplies dwindle and manufacturers maintain their price stance, futures prices are expected to gradually rise, allowing actual spot transaction prices to find a new balance between futures prices and prevailing spot offers.
Separately, an industry source said the China Photovoltaic Industry Association would organize monitoring activities to oversee the implementation of polysilicon production cuts planned for the fourth quarter, adding that this gives the market a degree of confidence and expectation that prices will remain stable. However, no official confirmation or disclosure regarding these activities was available at the time of reporting.
Looking ahead, an upstream participant expected mainstream polysilicon offers to remain unchanged until the Lunar New Year in early February 2027. Meanwhile, prices offered by manufacturers that have not signed the pricing self-discipline agreement, along with polysilicon futures prices, are expected to remain below mainstream spot offers.
The Global Polysilicon Marker (GPM), the benchmark for polysilicon produced outside China, was assessed at $19.234/kg, or $0.040/W, unchanged from the previous week.
Both manufacturers and buyers in the global polysilicon market continued to face mounting pressure. One trade participant noted that some suppliers had reduced their China-based polysilicon sales teams to just a handful of people, underscoring the increasingly weak demand environment.
On the demand side, a source at an integrated manufacturer said that certain long-term contract holders with cell manufacturing facilities in the U.S. could still absorb around 300 MT of global polysilicon per month. While this volume provides some support for demand, the contribution remains relatively small and limited in scope.
Certain long-term contract holders, despite being in poor financial condition, reportedly continue to purchase global polysilicon at a loss due to their contractual obligations. However, the pricing mechanisms embedded in long-term contracts negotiated several years ago have given buyers some room to negotiate, potentially allowing these agreements to remain in effect despite challenging market conditions.
In the near term, industry participants generally expect the main sources of global polysilicon supply to remain U.S.-produced material and lower-priced polysilicon from other origins. In addition, the framework established under the Section 232 outcome has enabled limited volumes of compliant Chinese polysilicon to continue flowing into Southeast Asia.
OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides energy prices, news, data, and analysis on gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG/NGL, coal, metals, and chemicals, as well as renewable fuels and environmental commodities. It acquired pricing data assets from Singapore Solar Exchange in 2022 and now publishes the OPIS APAC Solar Weekly Report .

articles.title_orig: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.title_zh: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.content_orig:
By SAM MERRIMAN, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 20:12 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 22:07 EDT, 1 November 2026
Ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China .
A report from MPs today criticises Labour's approach to Beijing as the 'worst of both worlds'.
In a devastating indictment of its dealings with the communist state, the chairman of the business, innovation, science and trade committee (Bist) said the 'Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along'.
Firms have missed out on lucrative commercial deals as Britain has been left increasingly exposed to 'unquantified, unmanaged risk', the report adds.
Last night the committee put pressure on the Prime Minister to clarify his stance on closer dealings with the Chinese Communist Party.
'We await confirmation of how much continuity there is between the approaches to China of the Starmer and Burnham governments,' the MPs said.
Last year Labour, under Sir Keir Starmer, refused to publish a Government review of relations with China, releasing only a short summary and arguing that publishing the full findings could damage British interests.
In June, two men were convicted of running 'shadow policing' operations on British soil, spying on Chinese dissidents and MPs who supported them.
Labour ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China. Pictured: PM Andy Burnham, then Mayor of Manchester, with China's Consul General Tang Rui on April 17, 2026
Labour's Ed Miliband shakes hands with Wang Hongzhi, head of China's National Energy Administration, at the China-UK Energy Dialogue in Beijing, China on March 17, 2025
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site were approved in January, despite spying fears. Pictured: A concept grapohic for the proposed embassy
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site near the Tower of London were approved in January, despite spying fears.
Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat has described the report as 'damning' and accused Labour of overseeing a dereliction of its duty to the public.
He told the Daily Mail: 'Labour are distracted and allowing Beijing to dictate terms, risking economic dependence on a hostile China. This is unacceptable. The Government's disjointed, last-minute approach leaves Britain weak and susceptible to Chinese control.'
The report warns that 'low-cost, increasingly sophisticated Chinese-connected technology has proliferated in the UK' and says the Government should create a register of high-risk firms to combat the threat associated with this.
It concludes: 'We are disappointed that, in failing to create a register of high-risk jurisdictions, the Government has prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security.' However, the Government last night rejected the Bist committee report and said it 'disagrees with its conclusion'.
The committee found that Labour has re-engaged with Beijing 'without establishing the rules of the game'.
Its chairman, Labour MP Liam Byrne, said: 'Businesses cannot plan for the future when the Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along. Ministers promised clarity and consistency.
'Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour. Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.'
China's President Xi Jinping, right, and Britain's then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, left, shake hands before their meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on January 29, 2026
Bill Yuen, 65, (l) and Peter Wai, 41, (r) were convicted in June following a trial at the Old Bailey. Wai was found guilty of running a Chinese 'state intelligence service' on British soil while working as a UK Border Force officer, on the orders of former Hong Kong superintendent Yuen
The report also found products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims ending up on British shelves. Pictured: Buildings north of Kashgar in China's northwestern Xinjiang region believed to be a re-education camp where mostly Muslim ethnic minorities are detained
Should Britain risk national security for economic ties and diplomatic relations with China?
Mr Byrne added that 'we should welcome trade that builds Britain's strength' but cease dealings that 'put that strength at risk'.
The committee recognised that disengaging from China is neither realistic nor desirable as annual trade with Beijing is now £140billion a year – about 7 per cent of total UK trade.
However it added that changes need to be made as the Government's decision-making on China – such as the takeover of British Steel from the firm's Chinese owners at a cost of £1.3million a day – has been characterised by 'reactivity, inconsistency, and opacity'.
MPs also raised concerns about the increasing adoption of cheap Chinese electric cars. These devices pose a risk to national security through spying and the ability to control vehicles remotely is a 'potential risk to life', the report adds.
The report is also damning on the risk of products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims in the Xinjiang region ending up on British shelves.
In order to reset Britain's relationship with China, MPs have called on the Government to 'insist on fair trade' to create a 'level playing field'. Ministers should also 'prevent the transfer of sensitive technologies and data to China'.
A Government spokesman said: 'Our approach to China is consistent – we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must.
'Our Trade Strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on national security. Increased discussions with China allow us to directly raise concerns where they arise.'
DAILY MAIL COMMENT: It's time to drop the 'diplomatic politeness' and change your tune on China, PM...

articles.title_orig: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.title_zh: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump said Washington had not “finished off” Iran because Tehran wanted to keep talking, while suggesting the United States might eventually take further action.
In an interview with Miranda Devine on the Pod Force One podcast, released Monday, Trump said: “We’ve been nice because we haven’t finished them off because, you know, they wanted to talk and they keep talking, talking, talking. At some point, we’ll have to do that.”
He added that Iran wanted to make a deal, but said, “We’ll see about a deal.”
Trump also said the United States could not allow Iran to have nuclear weapons.
Russia’s foreign ministry said on Monday that reports of new military action against Iran were a cause for extreme concern.
Moscow called for greater diplomatic efforts to normalize the situation in the region.
The United Arab Emirates will be better prepared than before for whatever follows in the US-Israeli war with Iran, Energy Minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said on Monday.
Speaking at the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference, he said the course of the war was unpredictable.
At certain points, he added, the UAE’s exports had performed better than before the war.
Iran’s position on defending its national security, sovereignty and territorial integrity has not changed, and Tehran will make no compromises on those issues, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said on Monday after meeting China’s foreign minister in Beijing.
Ali Bagheri Kani also described the killing of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by the United States and Israel as a “war crime.”
The spokesman for Iran parliament’s national security committee warned on Monday that a renewed war could spread geographically and strike areas not previously considered targets.
Hassan Ghashghavi said there were places “perhaps no one has thought about so far,” but said he would not discuss details.
He said Iran’s offensive and defensive capabilities had improved since the 12-day war and that a new conflict would bring “more surprises.”
Ghashghavi said an order by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei for an immediate and effective response to threats, without geographical limits, had been issued for implementation and should not remain at the level of analysis and commentary.
The gold, jewelry, silver and coin dealers’ union in Iran’s northeastern city of Mashhad has banned the sale and display of gold products featuring designs associated with the Pahlavi era or the Lion and Sun, according to an official notice to businesses in the sector.
The union said businesses found displaying or selling the items would face action.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Monday that parties to the Middle East conflict should pursue political solutions rather than resume fighting, during a meeting in Beijing with Iranian national security official Ali Bagheri Kani, China’s Xinhua news agency reported.
Wang also said China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security.
Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, but not because of difficulties in talks aimed at ending the US-Israeli war on Iran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing an official briefed on the discussions.
A draft proposal was being circulated for feedback, and a follow-up meeting was possible, the official added.
Iran should extend its missile range beyond 2,000 kilometers and reconsider its nuclear doctrine, including developing the capability to build nuclear weapons, a lawmaker said on Monday.
Mohammad Motamedizadeh said Israel was “at the tip of our blade” and that Iran should also target “the heart of America.” He said Iran could target adversaries’ interests in the United States and Europe if threatened.
He added that there was no reason for Iran to remain in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
He also described Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s remarks about responding to threats “at any level” as a sign of a shift in Iran’s nuclear posture.

articles.title_orig: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
articles.title_zh: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.
But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.
Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

articles.title_orig: Iranian Tankers Bypass U.S. Naval Blockade to Transport Gas to China
articles.title_zh: Iranian Tankers Bypass U.S. Naval Blockade to Transport Gas to China
articles.content_orig:
A report by Fox News, citing the advocacy group “United Against Nuclear Iran” (UANI), reveals that at least nine tankers carrying Iranian oil or liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) have successfully bypassed U.S. maritime restrictions since the reimposition of the American naval blockade in July 2026.
According to the report, published on the evening of Sunday, November 1, 2026, tankers belonging to the Islamic Republic’s so-called “ghost fleet” are utilising maritime routes around Malaysia to transport sanctioned Iranian energy cargoes to China.
Following months of investigation, UANI published images of a tanker named “SOGL,” which departed from the port of Asaluyeh in late August 2026, carrying approximately 500,000 barrels of liquefied petroleum gas. After breaking through the U.S. naval blockade, the vessel reached Malaysian waters.
Jemima Shelley, a senior analyst at UANI, told Fox News that the tanker refuelled in waters near Malaysia and, after receiving support services, delivered its cargo to the port of Qinzhou in China.
According to Shelley, some smaller Iranian tankers turn off their tracking systems, sail under false flags, or conduct ship-to-ship transfers at sea to evade detection.
The UANI analyst noted that while the U.S. blockade has severely curtailed Iran’s crude oil exports, certain smaller tankers still manage to slip through.
Fox News further reported that China now serves as the destination for almost “all of Iran’s oil and LPG exports,” with Malaysian maritime corridors playing a critical role in sustaining this trade.

articles.title_zh: China touts AI milestone: models generate more tokens than used in training
articles.content_orig:
Average daily token calls exceed 175 trillion, government-backed report says, indicating growing demand for AI services
For the first time, the amount of inference data generated by artificial intelligence systems in China has surpassed the amount of data used to train those systems, according to a new government-backed report, illustrating how the country is increasingly adopting AI at scale.
The report released on Saturday by the China Centre for Information Industry Development (CCID), which operates under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), cited recent official data showing that China’s average daily token calls exceeded 175 trillion, an increase of more than 1,000 times from early 2024.
Inference refers to the process of running trained AI models to respond to user requests, which involves processing units of data known as tokens. As AI adoption accelerates, the volume of token calls, which refers to AI usage through public cloud service providers, provides an indication of growing demand for AI services.

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine say emergency alert apps were hit by apparent cyber-attacks
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine say emergency alert apps were hit by apparent cyber-attacks
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia say their emergency warning apps have been hit by cyber-attacks, causing false alerts to be issued
Moscow says a "massive cyber-attack" has affected its app but insists its wider alert system is "operating as normal" . A Ukrainian espionage group claims the messages included fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia
This comes shortly after Ukraine's air raid warning app sent out false warnings of a radiation threat in Kyiv , following an apparent hack
Ukraine has blamed Russia for the hack on its app, while Moscow is yet to say who it believes is behind the cyber-attack on its system
The alerts in Ukraine were sent out just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in the front-line Kherson region, our Ukraine reporter Abdujalil Abdurasulov writes
Edited by Toby Mann and Yvette Tan
While we wait for further information on the apparent cyber attacks in Russia and Ukraine, here's the latest on the strikes that were reported overnight.
In a statement on Telegram, Russia's Ministry of Defence says it struck a Ukrainian military cargo vessel at sea 58km south of Odesa overnight.
It says the vessel was "delivering cargo intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces".
Another strike hit a storage site for Ukrainian missile launch systems in the Odesa village of Tuzly, it says.
Meanwhile, a Telegram channel for the city of Odesa says four people were injured in strikes in Odesa overnight. "All received prompt medical assistance," the update says.
It adds that two private homes, a garage and city infrastructure also sustained "significant damage".
The false alerts started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT) on Sunday, with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide, in Ukrainian.
Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48 , which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying". Oreshnik is the name of a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile capable of carrying nuclear or conventional warheads.
A third alert, at 22:49 , again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49 , a fourth alert stated there was a "street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
We don't know much about the alerts sent out in Russia. But as we reported earlier, a Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent, reporting from Kyiv
Ukraineâs air raid alert app usually warns of incoming Russian drones or missiles.
Last night it issued alerts of a radiological threat, a chemical attack and street fighting here in Kyiv.
The warnings were followed by all clear messages just over an hour later.
The air force issued a statement saying the app had been hacked and reassured citizens there was no imminent threat of nuclear war, blaming Russian interference.
Hours later, Russiaâs emergencies ministry claimed it had also suffered a cyber attack and said people were receiving emails containing fake information.
Itâs not clear if the two incidents are connected.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, has told the BBC the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko says Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, are used to "practically non-stop alerts".
"Secondly, this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions," he says.
"It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities," adds Merezhko, a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People party,
Russia and Ukraine both say their emergency alert systems have been hit by cyber-attacks. Here's what we know so far:
The BBC's Newsday programme has just spoken to Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, who describes the hacking of Ukraine's air strike alert system as "concerning".
âI think itâs the first time itâs happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it wonât be the last,â says Lin, who previously served on former US President Barack Obamaâs Commission on Enhancing National Cybersecurity.
âWe donât know how they did it yetâ¦ Maybe in the future theyâll be able to do it more but we just donât know yet.â
Russia and Ukraine have also exchanged strikes targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Russia said drone strikes hit an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight, which Ukrainian media identified as the Kstovo oil refinery.
The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region - home to the Kstovo plant - described a "massive" drone attack during the night and morning.
Gleb Nikitin said significant damage was sustained and warned of power outages and reduced hot water supplies. He said one woman was injured as a result of falling drone debris.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked Russian oil and gas sites in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. A Reuters report quoted him as saying the intensity of these strikes were "very high".
Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Aftermath of a Russian drone strike in Kramatorsk, Ukraine on 1 November
The fake alert sent to Russia's emergency app had warned users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of getting lively" also told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
Emergency alert apps in Ukraine and Russia have been hacked, according to reports.
The Ukraine government's Center for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account, saying one of the alerts was a "message in Russian about Oreshnik".
A few hours later, Moscow also said that its emergency alert app had been hit by a "massive cyber-attack" - but did not immediately say who might be behind it.
Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
It posted a picture showing some of the alerts that had showed up on Ukraine's air raid warning app and asked residents to "disregard" any "strange messages" they might see in the app.
The Russian emergencies ministry says its public alert system is "operating as normal", stressing that citizens are informed of alerts through multiple channels including sirens and loudspeakers, text messages, and TV and radio broadcasts, and that the app is "only an additional, ancillary news service".
"The hacking of the mobile app has not had, and cannot have, any impact on the operation of the public alert system," it said on its Telegram channel.
It said specialists were working to restore normal operation of the mobile app but the situation was "under control".
Abdujalil Abdurasulov Ukraine reporter
The false warnings were sent out just minutes before the end of a ceasefire in the Ukrainian frontline city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022.
The rare six-day ceasefire had allowed hundreds to evacuate from Oleshky, in a deal that was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV.
It was the longest a ceasefire has held since the start of Russiaâs full-scale invasion.

articles.title_orig: Gold rebounds above $3,900 as dip buyers return after October rout
articles.title_zh: Gold rebounds above $3,900 as dip buyers return after October rout
articles.content_orig:
Articles by Kitco News Wire were generated by Kitco's AI-assisted reporting workflow and reviewed by Kitco News editorial staff, with every claim independently verified before publication.
Kitco labels all AI-assisted content as part of our commitment to editorial transparency.
For questions or corrections, contact the Kitco News editorial team.
(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in late U.S. trading Friday, as a technology-led equity market selloff intensified liquidation pressure across precious metals, offsetting the support normally provided by falling Treasury yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Crude oil prices climbed more than 2% following another tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to inflation concerns and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive. Spot gold was trading near $3,879.90 an ounce, down $141.60, or 3.52%, while spot silver was trading near $49.015, down $3.150, or 6.06%, on the session.
Friday's U.S. economic reports presented a mixed picture of moderating wage growth and weakening regional manufacturing activity. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. The October Chicago purchasing managers' index declined to 55.3 from 58.8 in September, missing expectations near 56.1 but remaining above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction. Friday's softer wage and manufacturing readings followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product report, which showed the U.S. economy expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace , compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation accelerated to 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation increased to 3.1%, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressure.
Market positioning remains divided between resilient economic growth, persistent inflation and the growing risk of financial-market instability. The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday , with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Interest rate futures continued to reflect substantial expectations for further tightening in December, although Friday's moderating employment costs and sharp equity-market decline provided counterweights to the inflationary implications of strong GDP growth and higher energy prices. Treasury yields fell as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield retreating toward 4.93% and the two-year yield approaching 4.58%. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. The more actively traded January Brent contract advanced $2.63 to $113.43, while Nymex WTI futures increased $2.12, or 2.08%, to settle at $104.12. Brent gained approximately 13.6% during October, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting persistent concerns about Middle Eastern supply security and the inflationary consequences of the regional conflict.
For gold, the latest Hormuz attack reinforced underlying geopolitical demand, but higher crude prices also heightened the risk that inflation will remain persistent and the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy. The sharp decline in bullion despite falling Treasury yields indicates that broader financial-market liquidation was the more immediate influence on Friday's trading. Silver suffered considerably greater losses as weakness in precious metals coincided with concerns about industrial demand, equity-market valuations and restrictive financing conditions. The widening gold-silver ratio reflected silver's greater sensitivity to deteriorating risk sentiment and concerns about manufacturing activity.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Friday as disappointing corporate earnings and concerns about artificial intelligence-related investment triggered heavy selling in technology shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 1.1% to close at 51,770.31, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8% to 7,580.07, its largest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% to finish near 25,437, as weakness in semiconductor and major technology shares dominated trading. Intel plunged nearly 29% following disappointing profit guidance, while concerns surrounding Amazon's capital spending added to pressure on the technology sector. The Russell 2000 declined 1.7% to 2,811.84, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap growth companies. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also fell sharply, losing more than 2% as weakness in precious metals mining and other resource shares compounded the broader deterioration in risk sentiment.
European equity markets closed mostly lower Friday as technology-sector weakness and concerns about elevated energy prices weighed on investor sentiment. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined approximately 0.4% to 646.73, while Germany's DAX lost 0.9% to finish near 25,819. France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to approximately 7,962, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 outperformed, advancing 0.1% to around 10,736. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell approximately 1.2%, reflecting heavier losses among major continental companies. European technology shares were particularly weak as the U.S. semiconductor selloff affected global valuations, while higher crude prices added to concerns about inflation, corporate margins and the outlook for regional monetary policy. Despite Friday's losses, the Stoxx 600 finished October higher, reflecting gains earlier in the month.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher and settling at $104.12 a barrel, while December Brent crude futures finished at $117.64. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note declined toward the 4.93% area as demand for government bonds increased during the equity selloff. The U.S. dollar was comparatively firm, supported by defensive demand and expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve policy. ( Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Technically, spot gold bulls' next upside price objective is to push prices back above the $3,890.00 to $3,910.00 resistance zone, with a sustained recovery targeting $3,943.00 and then $3,975.00. Bears' next near-term downside price objective is to maintain prices below $3,890.00, with deeper downside targets at $3,800.00 and then $3,780.00. articles.title_orig: Gold Climbs Back From One-Year Low as Dip Buyers Arrest Slide
articles.title_zh: Gold Climbs Back From One-Year Low as Dip Buyers Arrest Slide
articles.content_orig:
Articles by Kitco News Wire were generated by Kitco's AI-assisted reporting workflow and reviewed by Kitco News editorial staff, with every claim independently verified before publication.
Kitco labels all AI-assisted content as part of our commitment to editorial transparency.
For questions or corrections, contact the Kitco News editorial team.
(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in late U.S. trading Friday, as a technology-led equity market selloff intensified liquidation pressure across precious metals, offsetting the support normally provided by falling Treasury yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Crude oil prices climbed more than 2% following another tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to inflation concerns and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive. Spot gold was trading near $3,879.90 an ounce, down $141.60, or 3.52%, while spot silver was trading near $49.015, down $3.150, or 6.06%, on the session.
Friday's U.S. economic reports presented a mixed picture of moderating wage growth and weakening regional manufacturing activity. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. The October Chicago purchasing managers' index declined to 55.3 from 58.8 in September, missing expectations near 56.1 but remaining above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction. Friday's softer wage and manufacturing readings followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product report, which showed the U.S. economy expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace , compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation accelerated to 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation increased to 3.1%, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressure.
Market positioning remains divided between resilient economic growth, persistent inflation and the growing risk of financial-market instability. The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday , with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Interest rate futures continued to reflect substantial expectations for further tightening in December, although Friday's moderating employment costs and sharp equity-market decline provided counterweights to the inflationary implications of strong GDP growth and higher energy prices. Treasury yields fell as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield retreating toward 4.93% and the two-year yield approaching 4.58%. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. The more actively traded January Brent contract advanced $2.63 to $113.43, while Nymex WTI futures increased $2.12, or 2.08%, to settle at $104.12. Brent gained approximately 13.6% during October, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting persistent concerns about Middle Eastern supply security and the inflationary consequences of the regional conflict.
For gold, the latest Hormuz attack reinforced underlying geopolitical demand, but higher crude prices also heightened the risk that inflation will remain persistent and the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy. The sharp decline in bullion despite falling Treasury yields indicates that broader financial-market liquidation was the more immediate influence on Friday's trading. Silver suffered considerably greater losses as weakness in precious metals coincided with concerns about industrial demand, equity-market valuations and restrictive financing conditions. The widening gold-silver ratio reflected silver's greater sensitivity to deteriorating risk sentiment and concerns about manufacturing activity.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Friday as disappointing corporate earnings and concerns about artificial intelligence-related investment triggered heavy selling in technology shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 1.1% to close at 51,770.31, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8% to 7,580.07, its largest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% to finish near 25,437, as weakness in semiconductor and major technology shares dominated trading. Intel plunged nearly 29% following disappointing profit guidance, while concerns surrounding Amazon's capital spending added to pressure on the technology sector. The Russell 2000 declined 1.7% to 2,811.84, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap growth companies. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also fell sharply, losing more than 2% as weakness in precious metals mining and other resource shares compounded the broader deterioration in risk sentiment.
European equity markets closed mostly lower Friday as technology-sector weakness and concerns about elevated energy prices weighed on investor sentiment. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined approximately 0.4% to 646.73, while Germany's DAX lost 0.9% to finish near 25,819. France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to approximately 7,962, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 outperformed, advancing 0.1% to around 10,736. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell approximately 1.2%, reflecting heavier losses among major continental companies. European technology shares were particularly weak as the U.S. semiconductor selloff affected global valuations, while higher crude prices added to concerns about inflation, corporate margins and the outlook for regional monetary policy. Despite Friday's losses, the Stoxx 600 finished October higher, reflecting gains earlier in the month.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher and settling at $104.12 a barrel, while December Brent crude futures finished at $117.64. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note declined toward the 4.93% area as demand for government bonds increased during the equity selloff. The U.S. dollar was comparatively firm, supported by defensive demand and expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve policy. ( Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Technically, spot gold bulls' next upside price objective is to push prices back above the $3,890.00 to $3,910.00 resistance zone, with a sustained recovery targeting $3,943.00 and then $3,975.00. Bears' next near-term downside price objective is to maintain prices below $3,890.00, with deeper downside targets at $3,800.00 and then $3,780.00.
